G1G	α, Ἀλφα	Alpha	G:N-LI	Alpha	**Α, α, ἄλφα** (which see), τό, indecl.,\n**alpha**, the first letter of the Greek alphabet. As a numeral, ά = 1, α = 1000. As a prefix, it appears to have at least two and perhaps three distinct senses:\n1. ἀ- (before a vowel, ἀν-) **negative**, as in ἄ-γνωστος, ἄ-δικος.\n2. ἀ-, ἁ- **copulative**, indicating community and fellowship, as in ἁ-πλοῦς, ἀ-κολουθέω, ἀ-δελφός.\n3. An **intensive** force (LS, s. α), as in ἀ-τενίζω is sometimes assumed (but see Boisacq, see word).\n(AS)

@G18
	ἀγαθός	agathos	G:A / G:ADV	good	**ἀγαθός**, -ή, -όν,\n[in LXX chiefly for טוֹב ;]\nin general, **good**, in physical and in moral sense, used of persons, things, acts, conditions, etc., applied to that which is regarded as "perfect in its kind, so as to produce pleasure and satisfaction, . . . that which, in itself good, is also at once for the good and the advantage of him who comes in contact with it" (Cremer, 3): γῆ, [[LUK.8.8|Luk.8:8]]; δένδρον, [[MAT.7.18|Mat.7:18]]; καρδία, [[LUK.8.15|Luk.8:15]]; δόσις, [[JAS.1.17|Jas.1:17]]; μέρις, [[LUK.10.42|Luk.10:42]]; ἔργον (frequently in Pl.), [[PHP.1.6|Php.1:6]]; ἐλπίς, [[2TH.2.16|2Th.2:16]]; θησαυρός, [[MAT.12.35|Mat.12:35]]; μνεία, [[1TH.3.6|1Th.3:6]] (cf. 2Ma.7:20); as subst., τὸ ἀ, that which is morally good, beneficial, acceptable to God, [[ROM.12.2|Rom.12:2]]; ἐργάζεσθαι τὸ ἀ, [[ROM.2.10|Rom.2:10]], [[EPH.4.28|Eph.4:28]]; πράσσειν, [[ROM.9.11|Rom.9:11]], [[2CO.5.10|2Co.5:10]]; διώκειν, [[1TH.5.15|1Th.5:15]]; μιμεῖσθαι, [[3JN.1.11|III Jo 11]]; κολλᾶσθαι τῷ ἀ, [[ROM.12.9|Rom.12:9]]; ερωτᾶν περὶ τοῦ ἀ., [[MAT.19.17|Mat.19:17]]; διάκονος εἰς τὸ ἀ., [[ROM.13.4|Rom.13:4]]; τὸ ἀ. σου, **thy favour, benefit**, Phm 14; pl., τὰ ἀ., of goods, possessions, [[LUK.12.18|Luk.12:18]]; of spiritual benefits, [[ROM.10.15|Rom.10:15]], [[HEB.9.11|Heb.9:11, 10:1]]. ἀ is opposite to πονηρός, [[MAT.5.45|Mat.5:45, 20:5]]; κακός, [[ROM.7.19|Rom.7:19]]; φαῦλος, [[ROM.9.11|Rom.9:11]], [[2CO.5.10|2Co.5:10]] (cf. MM, _VGT_, see word).\n_SYN._: καλός, δίκαιος. κ. properly refers to **goodliness** as manifested in form: ἀ. to inner excellence (cf. the cl. καλὸς κἀγαθός and ἐν καρδία κ. καὶ ἀ., [[LUK.8.15|Luk.8:15]]). In [[ROM.5.7|Rom.5:7]], where it is contrasted with δ., ἀ. implies a kindliness and attractiveness not necessarily possessed by the δίκαιος, who merely measures up to a high standard of rectitude (cf. ἀγαθωσύνη). @G25
	ἀγαπάω	agapaō	G:V	to love	**ἀγαπάω**, -ῶ,\n[in LXX chiefly for אהב ;]\n**to love**, to feel and exhibit esteem and goodwill to a person, to prize and delight in a thing.\n1. **Of human affection, to men**: τ. πλησίον, [[MAT.5.43|Mat.5:43]]; τ. ἐχθρούς, ib. 44; to Christ, [[JHN.8.42|Jhn.8:42]]; to God, [[MAT.22.37|Mat.22:37]]; with accusative of thing(s), [[LUK.11.43|Luk.11:43]], [[JHN.12.43|Jhn.12:43]], [[EPH.5.25|Eph.5:25]], [[2TI.4.8|II Tim 4:8, 10]], [[HEB.1.9|Heb.1:9]], [[1PE.2.17|1Pe.2:17, 3:10]], [[2PE.2.15|2Pe.2:15]], [[1JN.2.15|1Jn.2:15]], [[REV.12.11|Rev.12:11]].\n2. **Of divine love**;\n(a) **God's love**: to men, [[ROM.8.37|Rom.8:37]]; to Christ, [[JHN.3.35|Jhn.3:35]];\n(b) **Christ's love**: to men, [[MRK.10.21|Mrk.10:21]]; to God, [[JHN.14.31|Jhn.14:31]]; with cogn. accusative, [[JHN.17.26|Jhn.17:26]], [[EPH.2.4|Eph.2:4]].\n_SYN._: φιλέω. From its supposed etymology (Thayer, LS; but see also Boisacq) ἀ. is commonly understood properly to denote love based on esteem (diligo), as distinct from that expressed by φιλέω (amo), spontaneous natural affection, emotional and unreasoning. If this distinction holds, ἀ. is fitly used in NT of Christian love to God and man, the spiritual affection which follows the direction of the will, and which, therefore, unlike that feeling which is instinctive and unreasoned, can be commanded as a duty. (Cf. ἀγάπη, and _v_. Tr., _Syn_. §xii; Cremer, 9, 592; and esp. MM, _VGT_, see word) (AS)
@G26
	ἀγάπη	agapē	G:N-F	love	**ἀγάπη**, -ης, ἡ\n[in LXX for אַהֲבָה, which is also rendered by ἀγάπησις and φιλία ;]\n**love, goodwill, esteem**. Outside of bibl. and eccl. books, there is no clear instance (with Deiss., _LAE_, 18:4, 70:2, cf. the same writer in _Constr. Quar._, ii, 4; and with MM, _VGT_, see word, cf. Dr. Moulton in _Exp. Times_, xxvi, 3, 139). In NT, like ἀγαπάω, -ῶ,\n1. **Of men's love**:\n(a) to one another, [[JHN.13.35|Jhn.13:35]];\n(b) to God, [[1JN.2.5|1Jn.2:5]].\n2. **Of divine love**;\n(a) **God's love**: to men, [[ROM.5.8|Rom.5:8]]; to Christ, [[JHN.17.26|Jhn.17:26]];\n(b) **Christ's love to men**: [[ROM.8.35|Rom.8:35]].\n3. In pl., **love feasts**: [[JUD.1.12|Ju 12]] (_DB_, iii, 157).\n_SYN._: φιλία. ἀ., signifying properly (see: ἀγαπάω) love which chooses its object, is taken over from LXX, where its connotation is more general, into NT, and there used exclusively to express that spiritual bond of love between God and man and between man and man, in Christ, which is characteristic of Christianity. It is thusdistinct from φιλία, **friendship** ([[JAS.4.4|Jas.4:4]] only), στοργή, **natural affection** (in NT only in compounds, see: ἄστοργος) and ἔρως, **sexual love**, which is not used in NT, its place being taken by ἐπιθυμία. (Cf. ἀγαπάω; and see Abbott, _Essays_, 70f.; _DB_, vol. i., 555; Cremer, 13, 593; MM, _VGT_, see word). (AS)

	ἄν	an	G:COND	if	**ἄν**,\n_conditional particle_,\nwhich cannot usually be separately translated in English, its force depending on the constructions which contain it (see further, LS, see word; WM, §xlii; M, _Pr._, 165 ff.; MM, _VGT_, see word).\n1. In apodosis,\n(i) with indic, imperfect or aor., expressing what would be or would have been if (εἰ with impf., aor. or plpf.) some condition were or had been fulfilled: [[LUK.7.39|Luk.7:39 17:6]], [[JHN.5.46|Jhn.5:46]], [[GAL.1.10|Gal.1:10]], [[MAT.12.7|Mat.12:7 24:43]], [[1CO.2.8|1Co.2:8]], [[ACT.18.14|Act.18:14]], [[1JN.2.19|1Jn.2:19]], al. In hypothetical sentences, expressing unreality, ἄν (as often in late writers, more rarely in cl.) is omitted: [[JHN.8.39|Jhn.8:39 15:24 19:11]], [[ROM.7.7|Rom.7:7]], [[GAL.4.15|Gal.4:15]];\n(ii) with opt., inf., ptcp. @G2504
	κἀγώ	kagō	G:CONJ+G:P-1	and I	**κἀγώ** see: ἐγώ.\n**ἐγώ**, genitive, etc., ἐμοῦ, ἐμοί, ἐμέ (enclitic μου, μοι, με), pl. ἡμεῖς, -ῶν, -ῖν, -ᾶς,\n_of person(s) pron._\n**I**.\n(a) The nom. is usually emphatic, when expressed as subjc, as in [[MAT.3.11|Mat.3:11]], [[MRK.1.8|Mrk.1:8]], [[LUK.3.16|Luk.3:16]], al. But often there is no apparent emphasis, as [[MAT.10.16|Mat.10:16]], [[JHN.10.17|Jhn.10:17]]; ἰδοὺ ἐ. (= Heb. הִנֵּנִי, cf. [[1KI.3.8|1Ki.3:8]]), [[ACT.9.10|Act.9:10]]; ἐ. (like Heb. אֲנִי), **I am**, [[JHN.1.23|Jhn.1:23]] (LXX), [[ACT.7.32|Act.7:32]] (LXX).\n(b) The enclitic forms (see supr.) are used with nouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, where there is no emphasis: ἐν τ. πατρί μου, [[JHN.14.20|Jhn.14:20]]; μου τ. λόγους, [[MAT.7.24|Mat.7:24]]; ὀπίσω μου, [[MAT.3.11|Mat.3:11]]; ἰσχυρότερός μου, ib.; λέγει μοι, [[REV.5.5|Rev.5:5]]; also with the prep. πρός, as [[MRK.9.19|Mrk.9:19]], al. The full forms (ἐμοῦ, etc.) are used with the other prepositions, as δι᾽ ἐμοῦ, ἐν ἐμοί, εἰς ἐμέ, etc., also for emphasis, as [[LUK.10.16|Luk.10:16]], [[JHN.7.23|Jhn.7:23]], [[MRK.14.7|Mrk.14:7]], al.\n(with) The genitive μου and ἡμῶν are often used for the poss. pronouns ἐμός, ἡμέτερος: τ. λαόν μου, [[MAT.2.6|Mat.2:6]]; μου τῂ ἀπιστιᾳ, [[MRK.9.24|Mrk.9:24]].\n(d) τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί ( = Heb. מַה־לִי וָלָךְ, [[JDG.11.12|Jdg.11:12]], al.), i.e. **what have we in common**: [[MAT.8.29|Mat.8:29]], [[MRK.1.24|Mrk.1:24, 5:7]], [[LUK.8.28|Luk.8:28]], [[JHN.2.4|Jhn.2:4]]; τί γάρ μοι, [[1CO.5.2|1Co.5:2]].\n(e) The interchange of ἐγώ and ἡμεῖς, common in π., appears in Pauline Epp. (see M, _Pr._, 86f., M, _Th._, 131f.).\n(f) κἀγώ (= καὶ ἐγώ), **and I, even I, I also**: [[MAT.2.8|Mat.2:8]], [[LUK.2.48|Luk.2:48]], [[JHN.6.56|Jhn.6:56]], [[ROM.3.7|Rom.3:7]], [[1CO.7.40|1Co.7:40]], al.; κἀγώ . . . καί, **both . . . and**, [[JHN.7.28|Jhn.7:28]].\n(AS)

As prepositive article, **the**, prefixed,\n1. **to nouns unmodified**: ὁ θεός, τὸ φῶς, etc.; to abstract nouns, ἡ σοφία, etc., to pl. nouns which indicate a class, οἱ ἀλώπεκες, foxes, [[MAT.8.20|Mat.8:20]], al.; to an individual as representing a class, ὁ ἐργάτης, [[LUK.10.7|Luk.10:7]]; with nom. = voc. in addresses, [[MAT.11.26|Mat.11:26]], [[JHN.19.3|Jhn.19:3]], [[JAS.5.1|Jas.5:1]], al.; to things which pertain to one, ἡ χεῖρ, **his hand**, [[MRK.3.1|Mrk.3:1]]; to names of persons well known or already mentioned; usually to names of countries (originally adjectives), ἡ Ἰουδαία, etc.\n2. **To modified nouns**: with of person(s) pron. genitive, μοῦ, σοῦ, etc.; with poss. pron., ἐμός, σός, etc.; with adj. between the art. and the noun, ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος, [[MAT.12.35|Mat.12:35]]; the noun foll, by adj., both with art., ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός, [[JHN.10.11|Jhn.10:11]] (on ὁ ὄχλος πολύς, [[JHN.12.9|Jhn.12:9]], see M, _Pr._, 84); before adjectival phrases, ἡ κατ᾽ ἐκλογὴν πρόθεσις, [[ROM.9.11|Rom.9:11]].\n3. To Other parts of speech used as substantives;\n(a) **neuter adjectives**: τ. ἀγαθόν, etc.;\n(b) **cardinal numerals**: ὁ εἶς, οἷ δύο, etc.;\n(with) **participles**: ὁ βαπτίζων (= ὁ Βαπτιστής, [[MAT.14.2|Mat.14:2]]), [[MRK.6.14|Mrk.6:14]]; πᾶς ὁ, with ptcp., **every one who**, etc.;\n(d) **adverbs**: τὸ πέραν, τὰ νῦν, ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος;\n(e) **infinitives**: nom., τὸ θέλειν, [[ROM.7.18|Rom.7:18]], al.; genitive, τοῦ, after adjectives, ἄξιον τοῦ πορεύεσθαι, [[1CO.16.4|1Co.16:4]]; verbs, ἐλαχεν τοῦ θυμιᾶσαι, [[LUK.1.9|Luk.1:9]]; and frequently in a final sense, ἐξῆλθεν ὁ σπείρειν, [[MAT.13.3|Mat.13:3]] (on the artic. inf., see Bl., §71).\n4. In the neut. to sentences, **phrases or single words treated as a quotation**: τὸ Ἐι δύνῃ, [[MRK.9.23|Mrk.9:23]]; τὸ ἔτι ἅπαξ, [[HEB.12.27|Heb.12:27]]; τὸ ἀνέβη, [[EPH.4.9|Eph.4:9]], al.\n5. **To prepositional phrases**: οἱ ἀπὸ Ἰταλίας, [[HEB.13.24|Heb.13:24]]; οἱ ἐκ νόμου, [[ROM.4.14|Rom.4:14]]; neut. accusative absol., in adverbial phrases, τὸ καθ᾽ ἡμέραν, **daily**, [[LUK.11.3|Luk.11:3]]; τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, **as regards the flesh**, [[ROM.9.5|Rom.9:5]].\n6. To nouns in the genitive, denoting kinship, association, etc.: ὁ τοῦ, **the son of** (unless context indicates a different relationship), [[MAT.10.2|Mat.10:2]], al.; τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ, **the things that pertain to God**, [[MAT.16.23|Mat.16:23]]; τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης, [[ROM.14.19|Rom.14:19]] (cf. M, _Pr._, 81ff.; Bl, §§46, 47).\n(AS)

@G5181
	Τύραννος	Turannos	N:N-M-P	Tyrannus	1. **an absolute sovereign **, unlimited by law or constitution, (Herdotus Historicus), etc.: not applied to old hereditary sovereignties βασιλεῖαι); such as those of (Homer) or of Sparta; for the term rather regards the irregular way in which the power was **gained **, than the way in which it was **exercised **, being applied to the mild Pisistratus, but not to the despotic kings of Persia. However, the word soon came to imply reproach, like our **tyrant **, (Plato Philosophus), etc.\n2. in a wider sense, **the tyrant's son **, or **any member of his family **, (Sophocles Tragicus):—;so, ἡ τύραννος was both **the queen ** herself or **a princess **, (Euripides)\n3. τύραννος, ον, as _adjective_ **kingly, royal **, [_variant_ datesTragica Adespota\n4. **imperious, despotic **, (Thucydides); τύραννα δρᾶν (Sophocles Tragicus)\nτύραννος is probably from same Root as κύριος, κοίρανος. (ML)
